newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil bond issuers look again at German market.
newsitem.headline: Brazil bond issuers look again at German market.

text.p: Following the success of Brazil's 1.0 billion Deutsche mark Eurobond this week, top-name issuers that have concentrated in dollar deals were expected to take another look at the German market.

"We looked at getting into the German market one or two months ago and it seemed a little out of whack with other currencies," said Sergio Zappa, executive international director at retail bank Unibanco.
"As a result of the republic's deal, it is likely that Germany will become a natural alternative as we decide to do something," Zappa said.
Unibanco, which this year expects to at least match the $450 million in Eurobonds it placed in 1996, has no immediate plans to go to the market, Zappa said.
Unibanco and fellow Brazilian retail banks Safra and Bradesco last month launched three-year dollar deals at record-low spreads of between 190 and 220 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries.
Brazilian issuers are no strangers to the Deutsche mark market. Unibanco, for example, has three outstanding mark deals. But issuers say the German market had been expensive over the past few months.
The republic's success in pricing its 10-year mark deal at an impressive 230 bp over Bunds, however, could bring some quality borrowers back to the market, players said.
"Certainly there is now an attraction in doing a mark transaction," said an arranger on the bond origination desk of an international bank in Brazil.

But he added that launching bonds denominated in non-dollar currencies only made sense for larger issuers like bank and state-owned corporations that are familiar with arranging dollar-swap deals that allow issuers like Telebras or Petrobras and the financial institutions would now consider the Deutsche mark as an alternative but for others the swap transaction is too complicated," the arranger said.
Antonio Bornia, executive vice president of Banco Bradesco, said the bank might return to capital markets in May, when Bradesco's 150 million Deutsche mark bond comes due.

"We are not planning anything at this moment, but when we do we will certainly consider the German market. But like all other non-dollar currencies it would depend on the price of the swap," Bornia said.
Dollar deals accounted for 85 percent of all Brazilian Eurobond issues last year and few expect that to change considerably this year.

Brazil's economy is more closely tied to the United States and most issuers prefer to do business in dollars. Brazilian issuers are also more familiar with U.S. Treasury rates than European interest rates.
Still, Petrobras, Telebras and state development bank BNDES are expected to tap capital markets this year. In the past, they have often followed the sovereign's footsteps into global debt markets.
